title: What Is a Humanoid Foundation Model? An Introduction to GR00T N1 - Annika & Aastha
talk_summary: This is an introduction to NVIDIA's GR00T N1 humanoid robotics foundation model, covering the data pyramid (real teleoperation, synthetic simulation, internet video), a dual-system architecture (slow planner + fast 120Hz executor), and cross-embodiment generalization via an embodiment-specific action decoder. It is a robotics research overview, not an agent-software-engineering talk.

takeaways.what_they_do: They split the model into a slow 'System 2' planner that decomposes complex tasks and a fast 'System 1' executor (~120Hz) that acts on the plan, and crucially co-train both jointly rather than training components independently.
takeaways.evidence_quote: previously what used to happen was each of these components was trained independently and that resulted in some kind of disagreement between the two systems

takeaways.technique: Embodiment-specific adapter on a shared base
takeaways.what_they_do: A shared foundation model handles general knowledge, while a small embodiment-specific 'action decoder' translates outputs to the target robot; only the adapter is swapped per embodiment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you're giving it an action decoder which is specific to the embodiment that you're going to use

takeaways.technique: Data pyramid for scarce ground truth
takeaways.what_they_do: They rank data by cost/quality: tiny expensive real ground-truth at top, synthetic in the middle, cheap noisy internet data at bottom, and deliberately keep all tiers in one strategy rather than discarding the noisy tier.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we didn't want to completely discard it. It forms part of this cohesive data strategy

takeaways.technique: Imitation vs reward tradeoff for reviewer training
takeaways.what_they_do: They contrast imitation learning (bounded by expensive expert data, has a gold standard) with reinforcement learning (no gold standard, trial-and-error on reward, but sim-to-real gap).
takeaways.evidence_quote: with the imitation learning, you're severely bottlenecked by the expert data, which is quite expensive
